title: India Has Cancer Screening. Fewer Than 2 in 100 Women Have Ever Used It
excerpt: Population screening for oral, breast and cervical cancer has been offered to everyone over 30 since 2016, yet NFHS-5 found only 1.9% of women aged 30-49 had ever been screened for cervical cancer — and survival collapses when cancers are found late.
body:
• India's public programme has offered population-based screening for oral, breast and cervical cancer to everyone aged 30 and above since 2016 — but NFHS-5 (2019-21) found just 1.9% of women aged 30-49 had ever had a cervical screening test, 0.9% a breast examination and 0.9% an oral examination.
  • The cost of finding cancer late is measured in survival: five-year survival for breast cancer is 76.3% when found early and 14.9% at an advanced stage — a gap of more than 61 percentage points, per the Health Ministry's screening framework.
  • ICMR's National Cancer Registry Programme estimated 13.92 lakh new cancer cases in India in 2020, up from 13.25 lakh in 2018, with about 7.7 lakh cancer deaths in 2020.
  • What you can do: anyone aged 30 or above can ask for oral, breast and cervical screening through the public health system; a national HPV vaccination campaign launched in February 2026 offers a free single-dose vaccine to 14-year-old girls at government facilities.

Cancer in India is often found late. By the time many patients are diagnosed, the disease has already advanced, when treatment is harder and the chances of survival are lower, The Times of India reported in an explainer on the gap between India's screening system and its use. The screening exists. The patients, mostly, are not showing up for it.

The programme that is already there

The National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke — now the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD) — was launched in 2010 in 100 districts across 21 states. In 2016, population-based screening was added for everyone aged 30 and above. It covers hypertension, diabetes and three cancers: of the oral cavity, the cervix and the breast.

The uptake figures come from the fifth National Family Health Survey, conducted between 2019 and 2021, which asked adults aged 30 to 49 whether they had ever been screened for cancer. Among women, 1.9 per cent reported ever having had a cervical cancer screening test, 0.9 per cent a breast examination and 0.9 per cent an oral cavity examination. In some states, screening rates for cervical cancer were as low as 0.2 per cent, Mirror Now reported.

Why late detection changes everything

The Health Ministry's 2016 operational framework for cancer screening states the arithmetic plainly. Five-year survival for early-stage cancers is 60.2 per cent for oral, 76.3 per cent for breast and 73.2 per cent for cervical cancer. At an advanced stage, those figures fall to 3.3, 14.9 and 7.9 per cent respectively. In absolute terms, a breast cancer found early carries a survival rate more than 61 percentage points higher than one found late; for cervical cancer the gap is about 65 points. The figures come from a 2010 population-based study cited in the framework.

The scale behind those percentages is large. The Indian Council of Medical Research's National Cancer Registry Programme estimated 13.92 lakh new cancer cases in India in 2020, up from 13.25 lakh in 2018, and the Union Health Ministry placed figures before the Lok Sabha of about 7.7 lakh cancer deaths in 2020, according to the Times of India report.

Why patients arrive late

The explanation offered by the oncologist cited in the report, Dr Prasad, has two parts: India has no mandatory screening programme, and patients often ignore early signs, so they are diagnosed only when the disease is at an advanced stage. Experts cited in coverage of the data point to lack of public awareness as the primary barrier to early detection — the programme is offered, not promoted person by person, and early symptoms are easy to dismiss.

Prevention is moving, slowly

One newer line of defence is vaccination. The national HPV vaccination campaign was launched in February 2026. It offers a free, voluntary, single-dose vaccine to 14-year-old girls, with parental consent, at government health facilities. By September 11, 2026, more than 80 lakh doses had been administered, the ministry said. HPV vaccination addresses cervical cancer before it starts; screening addresses it after. For the reader with family in India, both routes run through the same public system — and both depend on someone deciding to walk in before there is a symptom, not after.
